title.text:
Open weights, file formats,
size and running cost

objects.text: What does it mean to own, host or rent a model?

Applied AI and Automation  |  Session 7 of 14
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome to Session 7. Last time you met the families of foundation models, and several of them you can download. That raises our question for today: what does it mean to own, host or rent a model?

A model you can download is a very large file of numbers, and its size, its licence and its file format decide the answer. I will show real file sizes that I measured on this machine, and you will leave with a decision sheet.

slides.notes: That question breaks into three things you will be able to do. You can tell open source from open weights and read a licence for the limits that matter. You can work out by hand how big a model file is. And you can choose rent, host or own for one of your own tasks and say why. Nothing here needs coding. The multiplication is the hardest step.

title.text: Your two hours: numbers first, then the decision

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x3.95_3e7e1829.png
objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: You do the memory sum by hand and fill the decision sheet yourself.

slides.notes:
To get you there, today has three big parts. First, thirty-five minutes on the ideas: what open weights means, what a weights file is, how its size comes from a simple multiplication, and why file formats and quantisation are different things. Then twenty-five minutes of demonstrations with real file sizes that I measured on this laptop.

After the break you work the memory sum on paper and fill a rent, host or own sheet for a task of your own.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  What is the difference between pretraining and post-training?
2.  What can a benchmark tell you about a model, and what can it not tell you?
3.  Name two things you can read on a model card.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 6. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. What is the difference between pretraining and post-training? Take a moment.

A good answer is this. Pretraining trains next-token prediction on a huge library of text, to learn the patterns of language. Post-training (supervised fine-tuning, instruction tuning, RLHF) trains further on examples of good answers, so the model follows instructions.

Question two. What can a benchmark tell you about a model, and what can it not tell you? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. It compares models on a standard set of questions, which helps a shortlist. It does not test your own documents or risks, so you test the finalists on your own examples.

Question three. Name two things you can read on a model card. Think about your own work as you answer.

A good answer is this. What the makers say the model is for, how it was built at a high level, how they tested it, its known limits and its licence.

If an answer was missing, last session’s take-away sheet or workbook page has it. Now to today.

title.text:
How today connects: what we
already have and what it feeds

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_chain_11.90x4.45_5408054f.png
objects.alt: How today connects to the sessions before and after it

objects.text: Each session is built on the ones before it.

slides.notes:
So where does today sit in the story? The dots along the top are the fifteen sessions, from the map at Session 0 to your plan at Session 14, and the gold one is today.

We already hold weights and biases are parameters from Session 1, GPT-2: 12 transformer blocks from Session 5 and families of foundation models from Session 6. Nothing today starts from zero.

What today adds is this: precision, quantisation, file formats, hosting.

And it feeds straight into what comes next. Session 8: how to prompt the model you have chosen. Keep that chain in mind, because each idea you learn today is a step on it.

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: Parameters are all the weights and biases of a model, the numbers training adjusts. Precision is the bits stored per parameter: FP32 is 32-bit floating point, FP16 is 16-bit.
Open weights: the trained parameters can be downloaded, under a licence that can still limit use. Open source (OSI definition) also needs the code and data information.
Lowering the number of bits per parameter, for example to INT8 (8-bit integers) or 4-bit, so the file shrinks.
How the parameters are packed in a file: safetensors, GGUF or ONNX. A format is not a precision.
Inference is using a trained model. Latency is the wait for an answer. Hosting is running a model on a server you rent.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_bars_0.70.png
/Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_key_0.70.png
/Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_calculator_0.66.png
/Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_folder_0.66.png
/Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_cloud_0.66.png

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Parameters and precision. Parameters are all the weights and biases of a model, the numbers training adjusts. Precision is the bits stored per parameter: FP32 is 32-bit floating point, FP16 is 16-bit.

Open weights and open source. Open weights: the trained parameters can be downloaded, under a licence that can still limit use. Open source (OSI definition) also needs the code and data information.

Quantisation. Lowering the number of bits per parameter, for example to INT8 (8-bit integers) or 4-bit, so the file shrinks.

File formats. How the parameters are packed in a file: safetensors, GGUF or ONNX. A format is not a precision.

Inference, latency, hosting. Inference is using a trained model. Latency is the wait for an answer. Hosting is running a model on a server you rent.

Keep those words close. The first idea uses them straight away, so let us begin.

title.text:
Parameters are the weights and biases of
Session 1: GPT-2 small has 124,439,808 of them

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t07_weights_link_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Parameters are the weights and biases of Session 1: GPT-2 small has 124,439,808 of them

objects.text: Parameters = weights + biases. GPT-2 count from demo_runs/s07/gpt2_count.py.

slides.notes:
Today one word comes up all the time, so let me build it from what you know. In Session 1, the house price was a weighted sum: w1 x1 plus w2 x2 plus b, with two weights and one bias, so three parameters. Each w is a weight, which says how much one input counts.

The b is the bias, a number added to the sum that shifts when the neuron switches on. All the weights and biases of a model together are its parameters, the numbers that training adjusts. The digit network had 1,210 of them. GPT-2 small, from Session 5, has twelve transformer blocks of 7,087,872 parameters each, plus its embedding matrix and position embeddings.

I counted every one: 124,439,808. Same kind of number, only many more. Now the first big question: who may download these parameters?

title.text:
Open weights means the parameters can
be downloaded; open source needs more

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t07_openness_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Open weights means the parameters can be downloaded; open source needs more

objects.text: The Open Source Initiative (OSI) definition of Open Source AI needs all four.

runs.text: Open weights: the trained parameters can be downloaded. The licence can still limit use.
OSI Open Source AI Definition 1.0 dates from 2024. Data information describes the training data; the data itself need not be shared.

slides.notes:
With parameters understood, the next two terms are open weights and open source. You will meet both in every vendor meeting, so let us make them exact. A licence is the legal permission that says what you may do with a model. Open weights means the trained parameters can be downloaded and run, under a licence that may still limit use.

Open source in the OSI sense is stricter. Think of a cake, as an analogy: open weights is the finished cake you may take home, and open source is the cake, the recipe and the shopping list, with permission to bake it for any purpose. The OSI definition asks for the parameters, the complete code to train and run the system, and enough information about the training data. Most downloadable models give you the first item only.

title.text:
A licence with conditions makes a model
open weights, however free the download

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t07_licence_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: A licence with conditions makes a model open weights, however free the download

objects.text: Llama 3.2 licence, read on 6 November 2026. Check the version in force.

slides.notes:
Even that first item can come with strings attached, so here is a real example. Meta lets you download its Llama parameters for free. The Llama 3.2 licence still has conditions. A company with more than 700 million monthly users must ask Meta for a licence. You must show Built with Llama if you distribute it, follow Meta’s Acceptable Use Policy, and start the name of a model made with it with the word Llama.

The Open Source Initiative said in 2023 that the Llama licence is not open source because it limits some users and some uses, and repeated this in February 2025 for Llama 3.x. So call such models open weights. This is not legal advice, so read the licence you will use.

title.text:
Inside a weights file: a table of numbers,
the parameters that training adjusted

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t07_weightsfile_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Inside a weights file: a table of numbers, the parameters that training adjusted

objects.text: A model file is a table of numbers. Each number is one parameter.

runs.text: Training adjusted each one a little at a time, as in Session 0.
This small model has 134,515,008 parameters, weights and biases together.

slides.notes:
With the labels sorted, let us look inside the file, so that size stops being a mystery. As an analogy, picture a mixing desk with 134 million sliders. The training loop of Session 0 moved every slider a little at a time, and the model file is the list of where each slider ended.

This grid is real. I read the first values from the first block of a small open model called SmolLM2, under the Apache 2.0 licence. Each number is a weight, the same kind as in Session 1. Counting the biases too gives its parameters: 134,515,008. The file holds no words and no documents.

If it is only numbers, its size is a counting problem, and you already know how to count the size of files.

title.text:
Any file is how many numbers it holds
times the bytes each number takes

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t07_everyday_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Any file is how many numbers it holds times the bytes each number takes

objects.text: A byte holds a whole number from 0 to 255. More bytes per number: finer detail, bigger file.

slides.notes:
Before we measure a model, a familiar case. Every file on your phone is numbers, and its size comes from a multiplication. A photo of 12 million pixels has three numbers per pixel, red, green and blue, at one byte each: 36 million bytes, so 36 megabytes before compression.

One minute of CD-quality music holds about five million numbers at two bytes each: 10.6 megabytes. A spreadsheet of a million numbers stored at eight bytes each is 8 megabytes. A saved JPEG or MP3 is smaller because it is compressed. If each number took more bytes, the file would grow and keep finer detail.

Hold on to that, because a model is also a very long list of numbers.

title.text:
A model file is the same sum:
parameters times bytes per parameter

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t07_memorysum_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: A model file is the same sum: parameters times bytes per parameter

objects.text: 134.5 million parameters times 4 bytes each is 538 MB.

runs.text: Formula: memory ≈ N × b, weights only. N parameters, b bytes each.
A bit is a 0 or a 1. Eight bits make a byte, so b = bits ÷ 8.
FP32 is 32 bits, so b = 4. FP16 is 16 bits, so b = 2.

slides.notes:
It is the photo sum again. Count the parameters, multiply by the bytes each one takes, and you have the file size. In symbols, memory is approximately N times b, where N is the number of parameters and b is the bytes per parameter. A bit is the smallest unit of storage, a 0 or a 1, and eight bits make one byte, so b is the bits divided by eight.

The common full-precision form is FP32, 32-bit floating point, a way of storing a number with a decimal part: 32 bits is four bytes. So 134.5 million times four is about 538 million bytes. I wrote the real file and measured it: 538,090,376 bytes, the small extra being the file header.

The same sum works for FP16, INT8 and 4-bit, as the boxes show.

title.text:
The same sum shows why big
models need big machines

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t07_scale_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: The same sum shows why big models need big machines

objects.text: Memory ≈ N × b, weights only: b = 2 bytes (FP16) or 0.5 byte (4-bit). Arithmetic only.

slides.notes:
This is where the same multiplication, N times b, gets uncomfortable for a laptop. One billion parameters at two bytes each, in FP16, is two gigabytes. Seven billion is fourteen. Seventy billion is one hundred and forty gigabytes, which no ordinary laptop holds. Halve the bytes and you halve the memory, and four bits is half a byte, so seventy billion shrinks to thirty-five gigabytes.

This is the arithmetic of the weights alone. Running a trained model to get an answer is called inference, and it needs working memory for your conversation on top, so real needs are higher. Do not trust any claim about running a model on a given machine until the sum has been done. But how can a parameter take half a byte at all?

title.text:
Everyday picture: rounding a price to
the nearest UGX 100 needs fewer digits

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t07_rounding_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Everyday picture: rounding a price to the nearest UGX 100 needs fewer digits

objects.text: An analogy for quantisation: fewer allowed values, a shorter number, a small error.

runs.text: UGX 4,837 to the nearest 100 is 4,800. The error is 37.
To the nearest 1,000 it is 5,000. Shorter still, and the error is 163.

slides.notes:
That is a fair question, and an everyday picture helps. Take a price of UGX 4,837. Round it to the nearest hundred shillings and you write 4,800: eleven possible values between 4,000 and 5,000, and an error of 37. Round it to the nearest thousand and you write 5,000: only two possible values, a shorter number, but an error of 163.

Fewer allowed values mean less to write down, and a bigger error. This is an analogy, and it breaks in one place. A model does not round to round numbers. It rounds each parameter to the nearest of a fixed set of evenly spaced levels, with a scale stored for each small group. That is quantisation.

title.text:
Quantisation lowers the bits per parameter:
INT8 allows 256 values, 4-bit allows 16

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t07_levels_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Quantisation lowers the bits per parameter: INT8 allows 256 values, 4-bit allows 16

objects.text: Each parameter is rounded to one of fewer allowed values.

runs.text: INT8 stores each parameter as an 8-bit integer: 256 values.
Fewer allowed values need fewer bits, so the file shrinks.
The rounding loses a little precision. That is the price of the smaller file.

slides.notes:
Now the real thing. Quantisation lowers the number of bits used for each parameter. With 8 bits, written INT8 for 8-bit integer, a parameter can take one of 256 values. With 4 bits it can take only 16. In the picture the parameter 0.37 is stored as 0.37 at FP32 and at 8 bits, and as 0.33 at 4 bits.

It is the price rounding again, only on a finer scale. Across 134 million parameters the small errors mostly cancel, but not always, and we measure that in a moment. Notice that quantisation is a choice about precision. It says nothing yet about the file format, which is the next question.

title.text:
Quantisation as a formula: store a whole
number q, read back an approximate x̂

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t07_quantformula_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Quantisation as a formula: store a whole number q, read back an approximate x̂

objects.text: Affine quantisation, toy numbers. The earlier picture used a −1 to 1 range, so its values differ.

slides.notes:
Here is the same idea as the formula called affine quantisation in industry. To store a number x, divide by the scale s, round, and add the zero point z: q equals round of x over s, plus z. To read it back: x hat equals s times q minus z.

The scale s is the step between neighbouring levels, and z is the whole number that stands for zero. Take s as 0.1 and z as 8. For 0.42, x over s is 4.2, which rounds to 4, plus 8 makes q equal 12. Read back, 0.1 times 4 is 0.4, an error of 0.02.

Minus 0.26 is stored as 5 and read back as minus 0.3. The number 0.64 is stored as 14 and read back as 0.6. No error exceeds half a step.

title.text:
File formats are containers: safetensors, GGUF
and ONNX. Precision is a separate choice

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t07_container_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: File formats are containers: safetensors, GGUF and ONNX. Precision is a separate choice

objects.text: GGUF is a file format. 4-bit is a precision. A GGUF file can hold either.

slides.notes:
You now have two ideas that people mix up: how many bits each parameter gets, and which file format packs them. Think of a letter saved as a Word file or as a PDF. The words are the same, and the format is only the container. The same holds here.

The safetensors format holds the parameters in a file built to load safely. GGUF holds the parameters with settings in one file, and local tools such as llama.cpp read it. ONNX, the Open Neural Network Exchange, holds the parameters with the calculation, so a model can move between tools.

Quantisation is the other row. A vendor who says we ship GGUF has told you the format and nothing about the size. Let me prove the two are separate.

title.text:
Same model, three file formats:
the size follows the precision

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t07_sizegrid_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Same model, three file formats: the size follows the precision

objects.text: At FP16 all three are about 270 MB. The 4-bit files differ: ask which method.

slides.notes:
The proof is in real file lists, read from Hugging Face today. This is the same small model in three formats. At FP16 it is about 270 megabytes in all three. At 8 bits it is between 135 and 145. The format did not change the size, the precision did.

At 4 bits the answers differ, from 76 for my own simple conversion to 105 for a GGUF file and up to 182 for one of the ONNX files. Those are different methods, and some keep parts of the model at higher precision. So when someone says 4-bit, ask which method and what the file size is. Next I will make the sizes myself, in front of you.

title.text:
Demonstration 1: one small
model, four precisions, measured

objects.text: I will show

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t07_sizes_7.30x3.90.png
objects.alt: Demonstration 1: one small model, four precisions, measured

objects.text: Watch for

runs.text: Recorded run, SmolLM2-135M, torch, 6 November 2026.
The areas follow the file sizes.
Four bits would give one eighth. The file is 14%, because the scales add about 8 MB.

slides.notes:
This is a recorded run, and you can watch me repeat it. Watch two things: the areas of the boxes follow the file sizes, and the last box is not quite what the arithmetic predicts. I loaded the small model, counted its parameters, and saved the same numbers four times: at FP32, FP16, INT8 and 4-bit. Then I asked the computer for the size of each file.

538 megabytes, 269, 135 and 76. Each step halves it, until the last one. Four bits should give one eighth, about 67 megabytes. The extra eight is the scale numbers that every small group of parameters carries, so it can be turned back into a number.

title.text:
Smaller costs some quality: INT8
barely moved, our rough 4-bit did

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t07_quality_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Smaller costs some quality: INT8 barely moved, our rough 4-bit did

objects.text: Recorded run: the same model, three test sentences.

runs.text: This is a very small model, and small models lose more when squeezed.
Published 4-bit methods are smarter than my rough one.
Test any shrunk model on your own cases.

slides.notes:
What did you see in those boxes? The sizes halved with the precision, and the last step was 14 percent, a little over the eighth the sum predicts. A smaller file raises a worry, though. Does shrinking cost anything?

I measured the average loss on three fixed sentences, the same next-token loss as in Session 5, and the three likeliest tokens after the capital city of Uganda is. At FP16 the results are identical to FP32. At INT8 they barely move. At 4 bits with my rough conversion the loss rises from 4.57 to 5.09 and the top token jumps to the, with 56 percent.

That is a tiny test, and published 4-bit methods keep key parts at higher precision. The lesson is to test a shrunk model on your own cases.

title.text:
Rent, host or own: who runs the
model and where your data sits

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t07_options_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Rent, host or own: who runs the model and where your data sits

objects.text: Inference: using the model. Latency: the wait for an answer. Hosting needs open weights.

slides.notes:
Size and quality tell you what a model costs to hold. The next question is who holds it, and who sees your data. As an analogy, think of getting to a meeting. Renting is taking a taxi, and you pay for each ride. Hosting is hiring a car with a driver by the day, and you pay whether it is busy or idle. Owning is buying the vehicle, and you pay for fuel, repairs and a driver.

For a model, renting means a vendor runs the inference and your data goes to the vendor. Hosting means you run an open weights model on a server you rent, in a place you choose. Owning means your own machines. Latency depends on the hardware in each case. More control needs more skills.

title.text:
Fixed costs beat pay-per-use
only above a certain volume

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t07_breakeven_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Fixed costs beat pay-per-use only above a certain volume

objects.text: Break-even volume = F ÷ (p - v).

runs.text: UGX: F = 3,000,000 a month, p = 1,000 a request, v about 0.

slides.notes:
More control has a price, and a finance manager will ask when it pays off. Compare a taxi with a monthly hire: the taxi wins for a few trips, and the hire wins above a certain number. The figures here are invented, to show the method, because real prices change often and I give none.

A rented service charges p, UGX 1,000 a request. A server you host costs F, UGX 3,000,000 a month whether it is busy or not, and v is what each request costs you to run, about nothing here. Break-even volume equals F divided by p minus v: 3,000.

Below 3,000 requests a month renting is cheaper. Above it, hosting wins, before skills and care. If each request costs you 200 to run, the divisor is 800 and the break-even is 3,750. Use your own quotes.

title.text: NVF would choose a different route for each task

rows.text: No private data; pay only for use
Customer names and orders leave the company
Read staff payroll and leave files
Sensitive data stays where you choose
Search a large private contract archive

slides.notes:
Let us put the data and the volume together on a real company before you try it yourself. Nile Valley Foods, or NVF, sells maize flour, sugar and cooking oil. Here is how it might think through four tasks, each in plain words. Public product reviews carry no private data, so renting is the simple answer. Customer emails hold names and orders, so rent only after you have read the vendor’s data terms.

Payroll and leave files are the most sensitive, so hosting keeps the data where you choose. A large private contract archive is confidential and used heavily every day, so hosting may also pay. These are first views. Your lawyer and your IT lead should confirm each one.

Four questions expose a
loose use of the word open

objects.text: Ask the vendor

runs.text: Open source or open weights?
Which licence and limits?
Which file format and precision?
Which hardware?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_check_0.75.png

objects.text: Listen for

runs.text: A licence you can read
A file size and bit count
A test on your own cases
Who updates and secures it

objects.text: No licence name and no file size means no decision yet.

slides.notes:
Whichever route you chose, someone will try to sell you something, so here is the checklist to carry into any vendor meeting. Ask whether the model is open source or open weights. Ask which licence it is under and which uses it limits. Ask which file format and which precision the file uses. Ask which hardware it needs. Then listen.

You want a named licence you can read, a file size and a bit count, a quality test on your own cases, and a clear owner for updates and security. If you hear only the word open, you have no decision yet. Session 13 turns this into the vendor question list. That checklist is the heart of what you keep today.
